correctness.rationale: Hall applied to t copies per agent is equivalent to the subset inequalities on agents: every set of copies uses the neighborhood of its projected agents and has size at most t times their count. |N(S)|=D|S|−e_G(S) counts each internal shared good once rather than twice. Every unmatched good can be placed with a nonapprover since n≥3 and support is at most two, giving exact equality; if n=2 this step need not work. The degree bound gives t*≥floor(D/2), so another bundle can contain at most D−t*≤t*+1 of any agent's approved goods; every optimal EQ allocation is EF1. Since m=nD−e_G(N), fixed positive λ entails a subset of at least two vertices with at least (λ−1)|S|+1 edges. Two vertices with 2λ−1 parallel edges and singleton fill achieve this lower edge threshold in every feasible layer. The λ=0 ratio is 1, the λ=1 ratio is larger, and the positive-layer expression increases strictly with λ, yielding the fixed-(n,D) optimum. Independently recoded check at /workspace/branches/231cf4c4-c615-41c9-a890-526e28f32348/independent_check.py: all 346 specified small multiplicity profiles, literal EF1 and exact matching, 34 exhaustive complete-assignment cases, and the explicit extremizers over 190 (n,D) pairs. The argument, not that finite sample, proves universal sharpness.

value.rationale: The result resolves a natural quantitative compatibility question on a two-support domain without laminarity: exact EQ can have a welfare cost, but adding EF1 at its optimum costs nothing further. The sharp penalty at every density layer and the explicit extremizers are useful beyond a routine matching feasibility check. The scope allows transfers to nonapprovers, so no efficient-allocation claim is inferred.
